p: Two great codices read 'new' for 'empty': the two words sounded alike.

why: In later Greek κενόν and καινόν were pronounced almost alike, so scribes confused them. 'Empty' (without effect) gives the sense the line needs; 'new' makes little sense.

p: The Plain departs from Swete here and follows Rahlfs's critical text: 'eternity,' not 'own nature.'

readings.w: Rahlfs's critical text (Septuaginta, 1935); KJV 'his own eternity'
Swete's text (Codex Vaticanus, B); Swete's footnotes, as given in the digital text, record no other reading for this word

why: With 'eternity' the two lines match: made 'for incorruption' and as the image of God's 'eternity.' Swete's reading, 'image of his own nature,' recalls Genesis 1:26-27 and also makes good sense. In Greek the phrase is τῆς ἰδίας ἀϊδιότητος. This site's suggestion, not a finding of the editors, is that a copyist lost the first letter of the second word after the like-sounding ἰδίας. The Latin reads 'ad imaginem similitudinis suae' (Douay 'to the image of his own likeness'), which matches neither Greek word directly.

p: The Greek says 'frost'; the Latin and the KJV say 'foam,' a Greek word one letter different.

readings.w: Swete's text (Codex Vaticanus, B) and Rahlfs's critical text
Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 5:15 'spuma gracilis'; Douay-Rheims and KJV 'a thin froth'

why: The Plain follows the Greek of both Swete and Rahlfs. The Latin and the KJV mean foam; the Greek word for foam, ἄχνη, differs from πάχνη, 'frost,' by one letter, so their translators may have read it, but no Greek copy with it is named in Swete's footnotes. Frost blown off by a storm is a fair picture, and it is the reading of the Greek texts.

t: All lawlessness, or the whole earth?
p: The Plain departs from Swete here, following the corrected Vaticanus, Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus.

readings.w: Correctors of Vaticanus, Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Alexandrinus (Swete's footnote: πασαν BᵃᵇℵA); Rahlfs's critical text; KJV 'the whole earth'
Swete's text (Codex Vaticanus, B), first hand

why: Swete prints πᾶσα, which does not agree with 'earth' in Greek; it would have to go with 'lawlessness' ('all lawlessness will lay waste the earth'), which is awkward. The correctors of Vaticanus and the other two codices read πᾶσαν, 'the whole earth.' The difference is one letter, and the meaning is nearly the same.
